task: Investigate the number of diagonals in a polygon with n sides. Find a general rule for the number of diagonals, and explain how you know it works.
text:
Investigating the diagonals of polygons

Introduction

In this investigation I want to find out how many diagonals a polygon with n sides has. A diagonal is a straight line that joins two vertices which are not next to each other, so the sides of the polygon are not counted. My aim is to collect data, find a pattern, write a general rule, explain why the rule works, and then test it on polygons that I did not use to build it.

Collecting the data

I drew convex polygons from a triangle up to an octagon and labelled the vertices A, B, C and so on. To avoid counting a diagonal twice I drew each one in a different colour, and I also counted in a systematic way: first all the diagonals from A, then only the new ones from B, then the new ones from C, and so on. My results are in this table.

n (number of sides): 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
D (number of diagonals): 0, 2, 5, 9, 14, 20

Finding the pattern

First I looked at the differences between neighbouring values of D. They are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. They are not constant, so the rule is not linear, but they go up by exactly 1 each time. The second differences are all 1. A sequence with a constant second difference is quadratic, so I expect D = an^2 + bn + c. For a quadratic the second difference is 2a, so 2a = 1 and a = 1/2.

To find b and c I used two points from the table.
n = 3: 0.5(9) + 3b + c = 0, so 4.5 + 3b + c = 0
n = 4: 0.5(16) + 4b + c = 2, so 8 + 4b + c = 2
Subtracting the first equation from the second gives 3.5 + b = 2, so b = -1.5. Then c = -4.5 - 3(-1.5) = 0.
So D = 0.5n^2 - 1.5n, which factorises to D = n(n - 3)/2.

I then checked this against the values I had not used to find it:
n = 5: 5 x 2 / 2 = 5
n = 6: 6 x 3 / 2 = 9
n = 7: 7 x 4 / 2 = 14
n = 8: 8 x 5 / 2 = 20
All four match my drawn results, so the rule is consistent with all of my data.

Why the rule works

I did not want to rely only on the algebra, so I looked for a reason. Take any one vertex. It can be joined to the other n - 1 vertices, but two of those are its neighbours and those lines are sides, not diagonals. So each vertex has n - 3 diagonals coming from it. With n vertices that gives n(n - 3), but this counts every diagonal twice, once from each of its ends, so I divide by 2. The number of diagonals is n(n - 3)/2, which is exactly the quadratic I found.

This also explains the differences. Going from n to n + 1 sides:
D(n + 1) - D(n) = [(n + 1)(n - 2) - n(n - 3)] / 2 = (n^2 - n - 2 - n^2 + 3n) / 2 = (2n - 2)/2 = n - 1
For n = 3 this gives 2, for n = 4 it gives 3, and so on, which matches the differences 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 that I found in the table.

Testing the rule on new polygons

The rule predicts 27 diagonals for n = 9 and 35 for n = 10. I drew a nonagon and a decagon and counted using the same vertex-by-vertex method. I got 27 and 35, so both predictions were correct. For a 12-sided polygon the rule gives 12 x 9 / 2 = 54. Drawing this one would be messy, so I checked it with the reasoning above instead: each of the 12 vertices has 9 diagonals, 12 x 9 = 108, and 108 / 2 = 54.

Using the rule backwards

Which polygon has 77 diagonals? I solve n(n - 3)/2 = 77, so n^2 - 3n - 154 = 0, which factorises as (n - 14)(n + 11) = 0. The negative answer is impossible for a number of sides, so n = 14. Check: 14 x 11 / 2 = 77.
Is there a polygon with exactly 100 diagonals? Then n^2 - 3n - 200 = 0. The discriminant is 9 + 800 = 809. Since 28^2 = 784 and 29^2 = 841, 809 is not a perfect square, so n is not a whole number and no polygon has exactly 100 diagonals.

Limitations

I only drew convex polygons. In a concave polygon some of the lines between vertices lie outside the shape. If a diagonal is defined as only a line inside the polygon, my rule would overcount for concave shapes. If a diagonal is any line between two vertices that are not neighbours, then the rule still works because it only depends on n. The rule is also only meaningful for whole numbers n of at least 3: for n = 2 it gives -1, which makes no sense.

Conclusion

The number of diagonals of an n-sided polygon is D = n(n - 3)/2. I found it from the pattern in my data, justified it by counting from each vertex, and tested it successfully on three new polygons. I also used it to answer questions about 77 and 100 diagonals.

task: Investigate the number of diagonals in a polygon with n sides. Find a general rule for the number of diagonals, and explain how you know it works.
text:
Diagonals in polygons

Introduction

For this investigation I had to find the number of diagonals in polygons. A polygon is a shape with straight sides and a diagonal is a line that goes from one corner to another corner that is not next to it. I wanted to find a rule that works for any polygon. I used a ruler and drew the shapes on squared paper so that they would be neat, and I put a dot on each vertex so that I could see the corners clearly.

Drawing the shapes

I started with a triangle. A triangle has 3 corners and every corner is next to the other two so there are no diagonals. Then I drew a square, which has 2 diagonals. Then I drew a pentagon and counted 5 diagonals. For the hexagon I counted 9 and for the heptagon I counted 14. I tried to draw an octagon too and I counted 21 diagonals.

Results table
Sides (n): 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
Diagonals (d): 0, 2, 5, 9, 14, 21

Looking for a pattern

I looked at how much the diagonals go up by each time. From 3 sides to 4 sides it goes up by 2, then 3, then 4, then 5, and then from 7 to 8 sides it goes up by 7. The 7 is strange because I expected 6 if it kept going up by one more each time. I think I might have drawn an extra line in my octagon by mistake because it was very messy with all the lines crossing in the middle. So the real pattern is that the amount it goes up by goes up by 1 each time, so the octagon should be 20.

Trying to find a rule

First I tried d = 2n but for n = 5 that gives 10 and the real answer is 5, so that was wrong. Then I tried d = n x n but this is much too big. Then I noticed that each corner has some lines coming out of it. In the pentagon each corner has 2 diagonals. In the hexagon each corner has 3. In the square each corner has 1. So the number of diagonals from each corner is n - 3. If there are n corners it would be n x (n - 3) but this gives 10 for the pentagon, and the real answer is 5, so you have to divide by 2. So my rule is

d = n(n - 3)/2

where d is the number of diagonals and n is the number of sides.

Testing the rule

n = 5: 5 x 2 = 10, divided by 2 = 5. This works.
n = 6: 6 x 3 = 18, divided by 2 = 9. This works.
n = 7: 7 x 4 = 28, divided by 2 = 14. This works.
For n = 8 the rule gives 8 x 5 = 40, and 40 / 2 = 20. This is different to the 21 that I counted but I think my drawing was wrong, so the rule is probably right.

I can use the rule to predict a shape I did not draw. A decagon has 10 sides so d = 10 x 7 / 2 = 35. I did not draw this one because it would take too long.

Why divide by 2

I divided by 2 because otherwise each diagonal is counted two times, once from each end. For example in the square the diagonal from A to C is also the diagonal from C to A.

Evaluation

My method was good because I drew the shapes carefully and I used a table to organise my results. The rule I found works for all of the shapes I drew except the octagon where I think I made a counting mistake. I did not test the rule on any shapes other than the ones I used to find it, apart from the decagon prediction. I also did not check if it works for shapes that are not regular, like a shape with one corner pushed in. I think it works for any polygon because I did not use the lengths of the sides anywhere. If I did this again I would draw the octagon again more carefully, with different colours for different corners.

Conclusion

In conclusion the rule for the number of diagonals is d = n(n - 3)/2. This works for all polygons that I tried and I explained why it works by counting the diagonals from each corner and dividing by two. The investigation helped me to see how patterns can be turned into a rule using algebra.

task: Plan A costs $12 per month plus $0.08 per minute, Plan B costs $4 per month plus $0.15 per minute, and Plan C costs $22 per month with unlimited minutes. A student's call log shows 132, 118, 145 and 125 minutes over four months; decide which plan is best, show your working, and comment on the accuracy of your answer and whether it makes sense.
text:
Choosing a mobile phone plan

The problem

A student has to choose between three phone plans. Her call log shows she used 132, 118, 145 and 125 minutes in the last four months. I will build a cost model for each plan, compare them, and decide which plan is best for her, then check my answer and say how far it can be trusted.

Setting up the models

Let m be the number of call minutes in a month and let the cost in dollars be A, B or C for each plan.
Plan A: A = 12 + 0.08m
Plan B: B = 4 + 0.15m
Plan C: C = 22 (it does not depend on m)
Plans A and B are linear models. The fixed charge is the y-intercept and the price per minute is the gradient. B has the lower fixed charge but the steeper gradient, so B should be cheaper for low usage and A should be cheaper for high usage. C is a horizontal line.

Finding where the plans cross

A and B cost the same when 12 + 0.08m = 4 + 0.15m
8 = 0.07m
m = 8 / 0.07 = 114.29 minutes (2 d.p.)
Check by substitution: A = 12 + 0.08(114.29) = 21.14 and B = 4 + 0.15(114.29) = 21.14. They agree, so the intersection is correct. B is cheaper below 114.29 minutes and A is cheaper above.

A and C cost the same when 12 + 0.08m = 22, so 0.08m = 10 and m = 125. B and C cost the same when 4 + 0.15m = 22, so 0.15m = 18 and m = 120.
Putting these together, the cheapest plan is:
- Plan B for fewer than 114.29 minutes
- Plan A for between 114.29 and 125 minutes
- Plan C for more than 125 minutes
At 120 minutes, for example, A = 21.60, B = 22.00, C = 22.00, which fits.

Applying it to the student's usage

Her mean usage is (132 + 118 + 145 + 125) / 4 = 520 / 4 = 130 minutes, which is above 125, so my intervals say Plan C is cheapest. At exactly 130 minutes: A = 12 + 10.40 = 22.40, B = 4 + 19.50 = 23.50, C = 22.00.

Because her usage changes from month to month, I also worked out each month separately.
Month 1 (132): A = 22.56, B = 23.80, C = 22.00
Month 2 (118): A = 21.44, B = 21.70, C = 22.00
Month 3 (145): A = 23.60, B = 25.75, C = 22.00
Month 4 (125): A = 22.00, B = 22.75, C = 22.00
Totals over four months: A = $89.60, B = $94.00, C = $88.00.
Plan C is cheapest overall, saving $1.60 compared with A and $6.00 compared with B. Over a year at 130 minutes per month, A would cost 12 x 22.40 = $268.80 and C would cost 12 x 22 = $264, a saving of $4.80.

Does the answer make sense?

Month 2 shows Plan A beating Plan C because 118 is below 125, and that agrees with my intervals, so the model is consistent with the actual data. The monthly figures are in dollars so I gave them to two decimal places. I did not round the crossover points until the end, so the rounding should not affect the totals.

However, the difference between the plans is small. Plan C saves only about 40 cents a month compared with A, and in two of her four months her usage was within 7 minutes of the point where A and C are equal at 125 minutes. If her usage drops by just 5 minutes a month, A becomes better. So my recommendation of C depends on usage staying stable.

Limitations of the model

I assumed the price per minute is constant and that minutes are charged exactly (in real plans, minutes are often rounded up to a whole minute, which would make A and B slightly more expensive). I also ignored data, texts, taxes, contract length and the price of the phone, which in real life could matter more than 40 cents a month. Four months is also a small sample.

Conclusion

I recommend Plan C. It was cheapest in total ($88.00 against $89.60 for A and $94.00 for B) and it is simpler because the bill is always the same. The advantage is small, so if she expects to talk for fewer than 125 minutes a month, Plan A would be the better choice, and if she expects fewer than about 114 minutes, Plan B.

task: Plan A costs $12 per month plus $0.08 per minute, Plan B costs $4 per month plus $0.15 per minute, and Plan C costs $22 per month with unlimited minutes. A student's call log shows 132, 118, 145 and 125 minutes over four months; decide which plan is best, show your working, and comment on the accuracy of your answer and whether it makes sense.
text:
Phone plans

I need to work out which phone plan is best for the student. I am going to make equations for each plan, work out where the plans are equal, and then use the call log to say which one she should pick.

Equations
Let m = minutes and let the cost be C.
Plan A: C = 12 + 0.08m
Plan B: C = 4 + 0.15m
Plan C: C = 22

Where are A and B equal?
12 + 0.08m = 4 + 0.15m
12 - 4 = 0.08m + 0.15m
8 = 0.23m
m = 8 / 0.23 = 34.8 minutes
So when m is 34.8 minutes they cost the same, and after that Plan A is cheaper than Plan B.

Using the call log
Total minutes = 132 + 118 + 145 + 125 = 520
Mean = 520 / 4 = 130 minutes per month

Plan A: 12 + 0.08 x 130 = 12 + 10.4 = 22.40
Plan B: 4 + 0.15 x 130 = 4 + 19.5 = 23.50
Plan C: 22

So for 130 minutes Plan C is cheapest at $22, then Plan A at $22.40, then Plan B at $23.50. Plan C saves her $0.40 a month compared to A. This matches what I found before because 130 is more than 34.8 so A is cheaper than B.

Does it make sense?
I think my answer makes sense because Plan C is a fixed price so she always knows what she will pay and it is cheaper than the other two. I rounded my answers to 2 decimal places because it is money. The answer for the intersection I rounded to 1 decimal place.

Limitations
I assumed that she uses the same number of minutes each month. In real life she might use more or less. The difference between the plans is only small so it might not matter very much which one she picks.

Conclusion
Plan C is the best plan for the student because it costs $22 per month, which is the cheapest at 130 minutes.

task: Investigate the maximum number of regions that n straight lines can divide a sheet of paper into, if every pair of lines must cross and no three lines may meet at a point. Find a general rule and justify it.
text:
Investigating regions made by lines

Introduction

In this investigation I was asked to find out how many regions a sheet of paper can be split into when you draw straight lines on it. The question said that every pair of lines has to cross each other and that no three lines are allowed to go through the same point. In this report I am going to explain what I did, I will show what I found out, and I will talk about the patterns that I noticed. I will also say what I think would happen if I carried on with more lines, and I will talk about how good my investigation was.

What I did

First I read the question carefully so that I understood what I had to do. The question wants me to draw lines and count the regions. A region is one of the parts that the paper is split into by the lines. I used a ruler so that my lines were straight, a pencil so that I could rub out mistakes, and a large piece of plain paper.

I started with one line, then I drew a second line and counted, then I drew a third and counted, and I kept going like this. Each time I drew a new line I made sure that it crossed all of the old lines, because the rule in the question says that every pair of lines must cross, and I also made sure that it did not go through a point where two lines had already crossed, because the rule says that no three lines can meet at a point. This was hard to do sometimes because the lines kept going through the same places, so I had to move them a little bit and start again. After I had drawn each new line I counted the regions carefully and then I counted them again a second time to make sure that I had not made a mistake. I wrote the number down every time.

My results

With 1 line there were 2 regions. With 2 lines there were 4 regions. With 3 lines there were 7 regions. With 4 lines there were 11 regions. With 5 lines there were 16 regions. I put all of these results in a table so that they would be easy to read.

Number of lines: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Number of regions: 2, 4, 7, 11, 16

Describing the pattern

When I looked at the table I saw that the number of regions goes up every time you add a line. This makes sense because every time you draw another line it cuts through some of the regions that are already there and makes them into more regions. I then looked at how much the number of regions went up by each time. From 1 line to 2 lines it went up by 2. From 2 lines to 3 lines it went up by 3. From 3 lines to 4 lines it went up by 4. From 4 lines to 5 lines it went up by 5. So the amount that it goes up by also goes up by one each time. I think this is quite an interesting pattern because it means that the numbers are growing faster and faster. It is not the same amount each time so it is not a simple times table pattern like the 2 times table or the 3 times table.

Making predictions

Using the pattern I can predict what would happen with more lines. For 6 lines the number of regions would go up by 6, so it would be 16 + 6 = 22. For 7 lines it would go up by 7, so it would be 22 + 7 = 29. For 8 lines it would go up by 8, so it would be 29 + 8 = 37. I did not draw 6 lines because the paper was getting very full and it was difficult to draw them without breaking the rule about three lines meeting at a point, but I think my prediction is probably right because the pattern has been working so far for all of the lines that I did draw.

Why does it happen?

I think it happens because each new line crosses all of the other lines and so it makes new regions. When I draw a new line it goes through the paper and cuts some of the regions into two parts. I am not completely sure exactly why the number of new regions is the same as the number of the line, but it seems to work every time. It might be because the lines are all crossing each other, but I could not work out the exact reason so I just used the pattern.

Evaluation of my investigation

I think my investigation was good because I followed all of the steps and I explained everything clearly. I used a table to show my results and I described the pattern in words. If I did the investigation again I would use a bigger piece of paper and different coloured pens.

Conclusion

In conclusion I found out that when you draw lines on a piece of paper so that they all cross, the number of regions goes up by one more each time you add a line. I started with the question and I did what it asked, I drew the lines, counted the regions and found a pattern. I think I explained my findings in a clear way. If I had more time I would draw more lines and I might also try what happens with lines that are parallel, or with curved lines, to see what the pattern would be. I would also like to try to find a rule, but I am not sure what the rule is because the pattern is not simple.

task: Investigate how many squares of all sizes there are in an n by n grid of squares, and write up your findings.
text:
Counting squares in a grid

Introduction

A chessboard looks as if it has 64 squares, but it has many more, because squares can also be made of several small squares joined together. In this investigation I will find how many squares of all sizes there are in an n by n grid, find a general rule, explain why it works and test it.

Collecting data

I drew grids from 1 by 1 up to 5 by 5 and counted the squares by size. For a 3 by 3 grid there are nine 1 by 1 squares, four 2 by 2 squares (their top left corners can be in 2 columns and 2 rows) and one 3 by 3 square, so the total is 9 + 4 + 1 = 14.
For n = 4: 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 30
For n = 5: 25 + 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 55
Grid size n: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Total squares S: 1, 5, 14, 30, 55

First pattern: sums of squares

In the breakdown the numbers are the square numbers added together. So S(n) = 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2. I can explain this. In an n by n grid a k by k square can have its top left corner in n - k + 1 columns and n - k + 1 rows, so there are (n - k + 1)^2 squares of size k. Adding over k = 1 to n gives n^2 + (n - 1)^2 + ... + 1^2, the same sum in reverse.

Second pattern: a rule without adding

Adding all the squares gets slow, so I looked for a direct formula using differences.
S: 1, 5, 14, 30, 55
First differences: 4, 9, 16, 25
Second differences: 5, 7, 9
Third differences: 2, 2
The third differences are constant, so S is a cubic: S = an^3 + bn^2 + cn + d. For a cubic the third difference is 6a, so 6a = 2 and a = 1/3. An empty grid (n = 0) has no squares so d = 0.
n = 1: 1/3 + b + c = 1, so b + c = 2/3
n = 2: 8/3 + 4b + 2c = 5, so 4b + 2c = 7/3
Doubling the first equation gives 2b + 2c = 4/3. Subtracting from the second: 2b = 7/3 - 4/3 = 1, so b = 1/2 and c = 2/3 - 1/2 = 1/6.
S = n^3/3 + n^2/2 + n/6 = (2n^3 + 3n^2 + n)/6 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6

Verification

Using the data: n = 3 gives 3 x 4 x 7 / 6 = 14, n = 4 gives 4 x 5 x 9 / 6 = 30, n = 5 gives 5 x 6 x 11 / 6 = 55.
New cases: n = 6 gives 6 x 7 x 13 / 6 = 91. Directly, 55 + 36 = 91. A chessboard, n = 8, gives 8 x 9 x 17 / 6 = 204, and directly 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36 + 49 + 64 = 204. So a chessboard has 204 squares of all sizes.
I can also check that the formula adds the right amount each time. S(n + 1) - S(n) = (n + 1)(n + 2)(2n + 3)/6 - n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 = (n + 1)[(2n^2 + 7n + 6) - (2n^2 + n)]/6 = (n + 1)(6n + 6)/6 = (n + 1)^2. This is the number of 1 by 1 squares in the new layer of squares, as the sum-of-squares pattern predicts.

Extension and limits

The formula is only for square grids. For an m by n rectangular grid with m not more than n, I think the number of squares is the sum from k = 1 to m of (m - k + 1)(n - k + 1). For a 2 by 3 grid: 2 x 3 + 1 x 2 = 8, and counting 6 small squares and 2 squares of size 2 by 2 gives 8, so it works. The formulas only apply to whole numbers n of at least 1.

Conclusion

The number of squares of all sizes in an n by n grid is n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, which is the sum of the first n square numbers. I found it from differences, explained it by counting squares of each size, and checked it on grids I had not used to build it.

task: A company models its profit P (in thousands of dollars) from producing x hundred items by P(x) = -2x^3 + 15x^2 - 24x - 10, for 0 <= x <= 6. Find the production level that maximises profit, justifying that it is a maximum and that no other value in the domain gives a greater profit, and find the range of production levels for which the company makes a profit.
text:
Part 1: maximum profit

Differentiate:
dP/dx = -6x^2 + 30x - 24

Stationary points occur where dP/dx = 0:
-6x^2 + 30x - 24 = 0
Divide by -6: x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0
(x - 1)(x - 4) = 0
So x = 1 or x = 4. Both lie inside the domain 0 <= x <= 6.

Nature of the stationary points. The second derivative is
d2P/dx2 = -12x + 30
At x = 1: -12 + 30 = 18 > 0, so this is a local minimum.
At x = 4: -48 + 30 = -18 < 0, so this is a local maximum.

Values of P:
P(1) = -2 + 15 - 24 - 10 = -21
P(4) = -2(64) + 15(16) - 24(4) - 10 = -128 + 240 - 96 - 10 = 6

A local maximum is not necessarily the greatest value on the whole domain, so I also check the end points, since the domain is closed:
P(0) = -10
P(6) = -2(216) + 15(36) - 24(6) - 10 = -432 + 540 - 144 - 10 = -46

Comparing all the candidates: P(0) = -10, P(1) = -21, P(4) = 6, P(6) = -46. The largest is P(4) = 6.

As a further check, dP/dx = -6(x - 1)(x - 4) is negative for x < 1, positive for 1 < x < 4 and negative for x > 4. So P decreases, then increases, then decreases, which agrees with a minimum at x = 1 and a maximum at x = 4.

Conclusion for part 1: the maximum profit on 0 <= x <= 6 is 6 thousand dollars, that is $6000, when x = 4, which is 400 items.

Part 2: the range of production for which the company makes a profit

The company makes a profit when P(x) > 0. Using my GDC to solve -2x^3 + 15x^2 - 24x - 10 = 0, I get x = -0.341, x = 3.09 and x = 4.76 (3 s.f.).
Check: the sum of the roots of a cubic ax^3 + bx^2 + ... is -b/a = -15/(-2) = 7.5, and -0.341 + 3.09 + 4.76 = 7.51, which agrees to rounding.
The root -0.341 is outside the domain. Since P(0) = -10 < 0 and P(4) = 6 > 0, P changes sign at 3.09 and again at 4.76, so P(x) > 0 for 3.09 < x < 4.76.

Interpretation. Because x is in hundreds of items, the company makes a profit when it produces between about 309 and 476 items (rounding the lower value up and the upper value down so that profit is guaranteed). If it makes fewer than 309 or more than 476 items it makes a loss. P(0) = -10 means that even with no production the model has a loss of $10 000, which I interpret as a fixed cost. The profit drops after 400 items, perhaps because of extra costs from running over capacity, so the best plan is to produce 400 items, but the maximum profit is small ($6000) compared with the size of the possible losses, for example -$46 000 at 600 items. The model is only valid for 0 <= x <= 6, so I cannot say what happens above 600 items.

task: A company models its profit P (in thousands of dollars) from producing x hundred items by P(x) = -2x^3 + 15x^2 - 24x - 10, for 0 <= x <= 6. Find the production level that maximises profit, justifying that it is a maximum and that no other value in the domain gives a greater profit, and find the range of production levels for which the company makes a profit.
text:
Finding max profit

P(x) = -2x^3 + 15x^2 - 24x - 10

P'(x) = -6x^2 + 30x - 24

Set to zero:
-6x^2 + 30x - 24 = 0
x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0
(x - 4)(x - 1) = 0
x = 4 or x = 1

To find which is max or min use second derivative
P''(x) = -12x + 30
When x = 4, P''(4) = -48 + 30 = -18. This is negative so x = 4 is a maximum.
When x = 1, P''(1) = -12 + 30 = 18. This is positive so x = 1 is a minimum.

Max profit:
P(4) = -2(4)^3 + 15(4)^2 - 24(4) - 10
= -128 + 240 - 96 - 10
= 6

So the maximum profit is 6 when x = 4, so the company should make 4 items to get the max profit.

Because x = 4 is a maximum no other value in the domain can give a greater profit.

Range of profit
I put the function in my calculator and looked at the graph. The graph is above the x axis between about x = 3 and x = 5. So the company makes a profit when x is between 3 and 5.

Final answer: they make a profit if they make between 3 and 5 items, and the max profit is 6 at 4 items.

Interpretation: This means that the company is good at making money if they make between 3 and 5 items. If they make less than 3 or more than 5 they will lose money so they should stay in this range. The profit is a positive number at the maximum so the company is making money, which makes sense for a company, and the second derivative test shows that the shape of the graph goes up and then comes down again so that 4 is the best.

text:
How quickly does my tea go cold? Modelling the cooling of a hot drink

1. Introduction and rationale

Most evenings I revise at my desk with a mug of tea, and most evenings I forget about it for twenty minutes and come back to a lukewarm disappointment. One night I noticed that the tea seemed to lose its heat quickly at first and then take ages to reach room temperature, and I wondered whether this behaviour could be described exactly. In physics we had met Newton's law of cooling, but only as a formula in a data booklet, with no data behind it. I wanted to find out whether the formula really describes a real mug of tea in my real kitchen, and if it does, to use it to answer a question I actually care about: how long do I have before my tea is too cold to enjoy?

My aim is therefore to collect my own cooling data, test whether a linear model or an exponential model fits better, use the better model to predict how long the tea stays at a pleasant temperature, and judge how far I can trust the model.

2. The mathematics behind the model

Newton's law of cooling says that the rate at which an object cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. If T is the temperature of the tea in degrees Celsius at time t minutes, and T_env is the room temperature, then

dT/dt = -k (T - T_env)

where k is a positive constant. I solved this by separating variables:

1/(T - T_env) dT = -k dt
ln(T - T_env) = -kt + c
T - T_env = A e^(-kt), where A = e^c
T = T_env + A e^(-kt)

At t = 0 the temperature is T0, so A = T0 - T_env. The model is therefore

T(t) = T_env + (T0 - T_env) e^(-kt)

The important prediction is that the excess temperature T - T_env decays exponentially. This gives me a test. Taking natural logarithms, ln(T - T_env) = ln A - kt, so a graph of ln(T - T_env) against t should be a straight line with gradient -k. That is a much better test than trying to judge by eye whether a curve is exponential.

3. Collecting the data

I made tea, poured 300 ml into a ceramic mug and left it on my kitchen table without stirring or covering it. I measured with a digital kitchen thermometer that reads to 0.1 degrees, although I think the real uncertainty is about 0.5 degrees because the probe moves slightly in the liquid. The room temperature at the start was 21.0 degrees. I took a reading every 2 minutes for 20 minutes and then every 5 minutes up to 30 minutes. Here are my readings and the transformed values.

t (min) | T (C) | T - 21 | ln(T - 21)
0 | 88.0 | 67.0 | 4.205
2 | 82.0 | 61.0 | 4.111
4 | 76.5 | 55.5 | 4.016
6 | 71.8 | 50.8 | 3.928
8 | 67.5 | 46.5 | 3.840
10 | 63.5 | 42.5 | 3.750
12 | 59.8 | 38.8 | 3.659
14 | 56.6 | 35.6 | 3.572
16 | 53.7 | 32.7 | 3.487
18 | 51.0 | 30.0 | 3.401
20 | 48.4 | 27.4 | 3.311
25 | 43.0 | 22.0 | 3.091
30 | 38.8 | 17.8 | 2.879

4. Analysis

4.1 First attempt: a linear model

The simplest model would be a straight line. The line through my first and last points has gradient (38.8 - 88.0)/30 = -1.64, so T = 88.0 - 1.64t. At t = 15 this predicts 63.4 degrees, but the readings at 14 and 16 minutes average 55.2 degrees, an error of more than 8 degrees. A least squares line on my GDC gave r^2 = 0.97, which sounds good, but when I plotted the residuals they formed a clear U shape: positive at the start and end and negative in the middle. That is the sign of a curved relationship, so a straight line is not the right type of model. A linear model also has a physical flaw: it predicts T = 0 at t = 88/1.64 = 53.7 minutes and negative temperatures after that, whereas a mug of tea in a 21 degree room can never cool below 21.

4.2 Exponential model

I plotted ln(T - 21) against t. The points lie very close to a straight line, and linear regression gave
ln(T - 21) = 4.20 - 0.0442t with r^2 = 0.999.
The residuals were all within 0.02, with no obvious curve. So k = 0.0442 per minute and A = e^4.20 = 66.7, which compares well with the measured T0 - T_env = 67.0. My model is

T(t) = 21 + 66.7 e^(-0.0442t)

Checking against the data directly:
t = 10: 21 + 66.7 e^(-0.442) = 21 + 66.7(0.6427) = 63.9, measured 63.5
t = 20: 21 + 66.7 e^(-0.884) = 21 + 66.7(0.4131) = 48.6, measured 48.4
t = 30: 21 + 66.7 e^(-1.326) = 21 + 66.7(0.2655) = 38.7, measured 38.8
All are within 0.5 degrees, which is the uncertainty of my thermometer.

5. Testing the model on new data

A model should be tested on data that were not used to build it. I kept the mug in the same place and took two more readings, at 40 and 50 minutes. The model predicts
T(40) = 21 + 66.7 e^(-1.768) = 21 + 66.7(0.1708) = 32.4
T(50) = 21 + 66.7 e^(-2.210) = 21 + 66.7(0.1097) = 28.3
and I measured 33.1 and 29.0. The errors are 0.7 degrees in each case, which is 2.1% and 2.4% of the measured values. Both measured values are higher than predicted, so the tea was cooling slightly slower late on than the model says. I think the main reason is that my room was not at constant temperature: the heating came on during the experiment and the room reached 21.8 degrees at the end.

6. Using the model

(a) When is the tea drinkable? I like my tea at 60 degrees or below, and I stop wanting it below 45 degrees. For T = 60:
66.7 e^(-0.0442t) = 39, so e^(-0.0442t) = 0.5847 and t = -ln(0.5847)/0.0442 = 0.5368/0.0442 = 12.1 minutes.
This agrees with my data, where the reading at 12 minutes was 59.8. For T = 45:
66.7 e^(-0.0442t) = 24, so e^(-0.0442t) = 0.3598 and t = 1.0225/0.0442 = 23.1 minutes.
So my tea is at a pleasant temperature for a window of about 11 minutes, from about 12 to 23 minutes after pouring. That is useful, because it tells me to start drinking when the tea has been poured for about 12 minutes if I want to avoid burning my tongue.

(b) Half life of the excess temperature. The time for T - T_env to halve is ln 2 / k = 0.693/0.0442 = 15.7 minutes. This is independent of the starting temperature, which I can check on my data: the excess is 67.0 at t = 0 and 33.5 at t = 15.7, and from the table the excess at 14 and 16 minutes is 35.6 and 32.7, which is consistent.

7. Sensitivity to the room temperature

My value of T_env is not certain, so I repeated the regression with T_env = 20 and T_env = 22. The gradients were -0.0429 and -0.0456, so k changed by about 3 to 4% for a change of 1 degree in room temperature. That is smaller than the uncertainty caused by the thermometer, but it shows why a stable room temperature matters. Using T_env = 20 would have made the ln graph curve slightly upward, and T_env = 22 slightly downward, which is another reason to trust the value of 21.

8. Evaluation

Strengths: the exponential model matched the data to within the uncertainty of the thermometer, it predicted new points to within about 2.5%, and its long term behaviour makes physical sense, since it approaches room temperature and never goes below it. The linear model failed on both counts.

Limitations:
- Newton's law assumes the cooling is proportional to T - T_env. A mug of tea also loses heat by evaporation, which is strongest when the tea is hot. My ln residuals are slightly negative between 2 and 25 minutes, meaning the tea was slightly cooler than the model predicted in this range, which is consistent with extra heat loss by evaporation, but I have not proved this.
- I assumed T_env was constant, but it drifted by 0.8 degrees.
- I used one trial. I cannot say how much k would vary between trials, and k depends on this mug, its volume and its surface area, so I cannot generalise the value 0.0442 to other drinks.
- The thermometer uncertainty of 0.5 degrees matters more at the end, where T - T_env is small (17.8 at 30 minutes), so the relative uncertainty in the later points is larger.

9. Reflection

The most useful thing I learned was how much the choice of graph matters. My first attempt was to plot ln(T) rather than ln(T - T_env), and it gave a curve, not a line, so for an hour I thought the model had failed. I realised that Newton's law is about the difference from the surroundings, and when I subtracted T_env the line appeared. That mistake made me understand the meaning of the model more deeply than I would have done by just using the formula. I was also surprised that the linear model had r^2 = 0.97 and still gave an 8 degree error: a high r^2 does not mean a good model, and looking at the residuals was what exposed it.

If I did this again I would repeat the experiment three times, record the room temperature every 5 minutes, and compare a mug with a lid and without a lid to see how k changes. I would also like to test the idea about evaporation by adding a second term to the model. I started this exploration just wanting to know why my tea goes cold, and I finished with a way of predicting it, which I have already used: I now start my tea at about 12 minutes.

10. Conclusion

The cooling of my tea is well modelled by T(t) = 21 + 66.7 e^(-0.0442t), with the tea reaching 60 degrees after about 12 minutes and 45 degrees after about 23 minutes. The model predicted new data within 2.5%, but it depends on the mug, and on a constant room temperature.

Sources: Newton's law of cooling in my Physics data booklet and class notes; my own measurements.

text:
Maths and football: what is the best place to shoot from?

Introduction

I play football for my school team and I am usually a striker. When I play I often wonder where the best place is to shoot from, because sometimes I take a shot from far away at a small gap and sometimes I take a shot from near the goal. I thought it would be good to find out if maths can tell me where the best place to shoot is. I think this is a good topic for my exploration because I like football and it is something I do every week. My aim is to investigate how the angle of the goal that I can see changes with where I stand, because a bigger angle means more space to aim at.

Background

A football goal is 7.32 metres wide. I will say the posts are at points A and B and the player is at a point P. The angle APB is the shooting angle. If this angle is big then the goal looks big to the player and it is easier to score. To work out the angle I will use right angled triangles and trigonometry (SOH CAH TOA), in particular tan = opposite / adjacent and the inverse tan function on my calculator.

Case 1: standing straight in front of the goal

First I look at the player standing straight in front of the middle of the goal at a distance d metres from the goal line. This makes an isosceles triangle. If I split it down the middle I get a right angled triangle with opposite side 3.66 (half the goal) and adjacent side d. So

tan(half angle) = 3.66 / d
shooting angle = 2 x tan^-1(3.66 / d)

I put some distances into this and calculated the angles.

d = 2: 2 x tan^-1(1.83) = 2 x 61.4 = 122.8 degrees
d = 5: 2 x tan^-1(0.732) = 2 x 36.2 = 72.4 degrees
d = 8: 2 x tan^-1(0.4575) = 2 x 24.6 = 49.2 degrees
d = 11: 2 x tan^-1(0.3327) = 2 x 18.4 = 36.8 degrees
d = 15: 2 x tan^-1(0.244) = 2 x 13.7 = 27.4 degrees
d = 20: 2 x tan^-1(0.183) = 2 x 10.4 = 20.7 degrees
d = 30: 2 x tan^-1(0.122) = 2 x 6.96 = 13.9 degrees

You can see that the angle gets smaller as you go further away. I tried to find out how it changes. For the bigger distances the angle times the distance is about 400. For example 11 x 36.8 = 405, 15 x 27.4 = 411 and 20 x 20.7 = 414, 30 x 13.9 = 417. So I think the angle is about 400 divided by d. It does not work for small distances, for example at d = 2 the rule gives 200 but the real angle is 122.8, so the rule is only roughly right and I am not sure why it works for the longer distances.

I also looked at the penalty spot, which is 11 metres from the goal line. The shooting angle is 36.8 degrees. That is less than half of the angle at 5 metres, which is 72.4.

Case 2: standing to the side

Now I look at what happens if the player moves to the side. Suppose the player is d metres from the goal line and x metres from the centre line, with x bigger than 3.66 so that the player is outside the posts. The angle to the far post is tan^-1((x + 3.66) / d) and the angle to the near post is tan^-1((x - 3.66) / d), both measured from the goal line direction. The shooting angle is the difference between them.

angle = tan^-1((x + 3.66) / d) - tan^-1((x - 3.66) / d)

I used d = 11 and tried different values of x. When x = 0 it is the same as case 1 so the angle is 36.8.

x = 3.66 (level with the post): tan^-1(7.32 / 11) = 33.6 degrees (the near post angle is 0)
x = 6: tan^-1(9.66 / 11) - tan^-1(2.34 / 11) = 41.3 - 12.0 = 29.3 degrees
x = 10: tan^-1(13.66 / 11) - tan^-1(6.34 / 11) = 51.1 - 29.9 = 21.2 degrees
x = 15: tan^-1(18.66 / 11) - tan^-1(11.34 / 11) = 59.5 - 45.9 = 13.6 degrees

So the angle gets smaller as the player moves to the side. I can see that the biggest angle for d = 11 is in the middle where x = 0.

I also checked my numbers using GeoGebra. I put in the points A and B and moved P around and the angle changed in the same way as in my calculations. I noticed that all the points that have the same angle seem to make a curve, like part of a circle through the two posts. I did not have time to investigate this but it is interesting.

Conclusion from the two cases

My results show that the best place to shoot from is as close to the goal as possible and in the middle. The angle gets smaller when you go further back, and it also gets smaller when you go to the side. This is what I expected, but now I have numbers to show it. At the penalty spot the angle is 36.8 degrees and at 20 metres it is only 20.7 degrees, so shots from far away are harder.

Evaluation

My method worked because I used trigonometry properly and I checked with GeoGebra. However there are some limitations. First, I only looked at the angle, but the goalkeeper stands in the goal and takes up some of the space, so a big angle is not always best. Second, in a real game a player can not always stand in the best place, because defenders are there. Third, I only used d = 11 for the case where the player moves to the side, and I could have used other distances. I also did not use real data from matches to see where goals are really scored from.

Reflection

I learned that trigonometry is useful in sport and not just in school. I found the inverse tan calculation interesting. In the future I would like to include the goalkeeper in my model and look at real data of goals. I enjoyed this exploration because I could connect maths to something that I enjoy.

Bibliography
FIFA laws of the game (goal size is 7.32 m by 2.44 m).

text:
The Golden Ratio in the Human Body

Introduction

I have chosen the golden ratio for my maths exploration because I think it is very interesting that there is a special number in nature and art. The golden ratio is about 1.618 and it is also called phi. It is found in many places such as the Parthenon in Greece, the Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci, sunflowers and shells. I wanted to find out if the golden ratio is also in the human body, because some people say that it is.

What is the golden ratio

The golden ratio is when you divide a line into two parts so that the whole line divided by the long part is the same as the long part divided by the short part. This gives the number 1.618. It is related to the Fibonacci sequence which goes 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34. If you divide one number by the one before it you get close to 1.618. For example 8 / 5 = 1.6 and 13 / 8 = 1.625 and 21 / 13 = 1.615. So the numbers get closer to the golden ratio.

My experiment

I measured the height of 6 people and the height of their belly button from the floor. Then I divided the height by the belly button height to get the ratio. If the golden ratio is in the body then the answer should be about 1.618. Here are my results.

Person | Height (cm) | Belly button height (cm) | Ratio
Me | 165 | 102 | 1.62
Dad | 178 | 108 | 1.65
Mum | 160 | 99 | 1.62
Friend 1 | 170 | 104 | 1.63
Friend 2 | 182 | 113 | 1.61
Friend 3 | 158 | 100 | 1.58

The average of the ratios is 1.618.

I also measured my forearm and my hand but I did not have time to do this for everyone. My forearm is 25 cm and my hand is 16 cm so 25 / 16 = 1.56 which is quite close.

Results and analysis

As you can see all of the ratios are close to 1.6 and the average is 1.618, which is exactly the golden ratio. This proves that the golden ratio is in the human body. The ratio of my forearm to my hand is also close to the golden ratio. So I can say that my hypothesis was right and the human body is made using the golden ratio. This is amazing because it means that maths is in everything and nature has a plan.

Evaluation

My investigation went well because I got a result that matched what I thought. Some of my measurements might not be exact because I used a ruler and it was hard to measure the belly button height. I could have measured more people.

Conclusion

In conclusion the golden ratio is found in the human body. I learned that maths is everywhere and I enjoyed doing this exploration.

Bibliography
Google, Wikipedia
